title: Not the Bat, Not the Owl: The Animal With the Best Hearing on Earth
description: Animal Secrets #24. Which animal has the best hearing on Earth? We count down five super ears, from a shark that hears you from nearly 250 feet away to an owl that hunts in total darkness, and a tiny moth that hears 300,000 hertz. Then the twist: a huge new study in Science (November 2026) shows human noise changes the body or behavior of 80% of the species studied. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: An owl can catch a mouse in total darkness. Using only its ears. And it's not even number one.

scenes.label: Not the bat?
scenes.say: So who has the best hearing on Earth? Most people say the bat. Okay, the bat is close. But it loses.
Today, five animals with hearing so good it sounds fake. Each one is crazier than the last.

scenes.label: Wait for #1
scenes.say: And wait until number one. It's a tiny bug that hears higher than any bat can even scream.
Then, at the very end, the twist. Because a huge study from this month says we're breaking these superpowers. Right now.

scenes.label: You: ~20 kHz
scenes.say: Quick reference first. Your ears top out around 20,000 hertz. That's the highest squeak a healthy young human can hear.

scenes.label: Cat: ~64 kHz
scenes.say: A cat goes up to about 64,000. Keep those numbers in your head. You're going to need them.

scenes.label: Blacktip shark
scenes.say: Number five. A shark with no ears you can see. No swim bladder either, the gas bag fish use to pick up sound.

scenes.label: Palm Beach, Florida
scenes.say: Every winter, huge groups of blacktips gather off Palm Beach County in Florida. Clear, shallow water. Perfect for spying on them.
So how good can it hear? Nobody really knew. Until scientists in Florida tried something clever.

scenes.label: Speaker + drone
scenes.say: They dropped an underwater speaker near wild blacktip sharks. Then they watched from the sky with a drone.

scenes.label: 100–800 Hz
scenes.say: They played deep, low sounds, between 100 and 800 hertz. Loud ones, meant to startle, not attract.

scenes.label: ~250 feet away
scenes.say: And the sharks spun around and swam away. Even from about 74 meters off. That's nearly 250 feet.

scenes.label: 10 kHz: nothing
scenes.say: Here's the wild part. They also played a high 10,000 hertz tone as a test. That's outside a shark's known hearing range.

scenes.label: Lower = better
scenes.say: And the lower the sound, the better they picked it up. Deep, booming sounds are what sharks are tuned for.
So sharks hear with their inner ears, using a structure called the macula neglecta. They feel sound as tiny movements in the water.
Why do it in the ocean? The lead scientist said a lab tank is like a house of mirrors. Sound just bounces everywhere.
So the next time you're splashing in the sea? Something out there may hear you long before you ever see it.

scenes.label: Hears with feet?
scenes.say: Number four goes the opposite way. Super low. An animal that may hear with its feet.

scenes.label: 20–40 Hz rumbles
scenes.say: Elephants make deep rumbles, around 20 to 40 hertz and even lower. Some of it is too low for you to hear at all.
But those rumbles don't just travel through the air. They shake the ground, too.
Stanford researcher Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell found these vibrations race through the soil. Like a tiny earthquake made by a voice.

scenes.label: 1 jump, 1 km
scenes.say: How strong can ground signals get? In one test, a single person jumping made a vibration you could measure a kilometer away.

scenes.label: Sensors in feet
scenes.say: And elephant feet are packed with touch sensors called Pacinian corpuscles. Scientists think vibrations travel up the bones to the ear, too.

scenes.label: Up to 2 km
scenes.say: In the wild, elephants reacted to played-back rumbles from up to 2 kilometers away. Over a mile.

scenes.label: Who's calling?
scenes.say: Even better, elephants could tell apart the same alarm call made by different elephants. Through the ground. Like recognizing a friend's footsteps.

scenes.label: Up to 16 km?
scenes.say: And her models suggest the ground signal of a rumble could be picked up up to 16 kilometers away. Footsteps, up to 32. That's a model's prediction, not proven yet.
Now think about that. An elephant standing still may be listening to a herd it can't even see.
Okay, but here's a question. What if you had to hunt in pitch black? No light at all?

scenes.label: Total darkness
scenes.say: Number three. The barn owl. In 1958, scientists showed it can catch a mouse in complete darkness.
No moonlight. No starlight. Nothing. Just the rustle of tiny feet in the leaves.

scenes.label: Under 1 degree
scenes.say: Later tests found its aim was off by less than one degree. That's about the width of your little finger at arm's length.

scenes.label: Lopsided ears
scenes.say: The secret? Its ears are lopsided. One ear sits higher than the other. Yeah, really.
So a sound from below hits each ear a little differently. The owl's brain uses that to work out up and down, not just left and right.

scenes.label: Tuned for mice
scenes.say: Its ears are tuned sharpest around 5,500 to 9,500 hertz. That's right where rustling leaves and squeaky mice live.

scenes.label: Feather dish
scenes.say: And that heart-shaped face? It's a dish made of feathers. It funnels sound straight into those ears.

scenes.label: ~4 m per second
scenes.say: In the dark it flies at about 4 meters per second. Then, right before impact, it swings its feet forward.
And often, it closes its eyes for the strike. It doesn't need them. It already knows where the mouse is.
That's why barn owls can even dive into snow after prey they can't see. Their ears do the looking.

scenes.label: The bat
scenes.say: Number two. The bat. You knew it was coming. But you probably don't know how high it goes.

scenes.label: Echolocation
scenes.say: Bats shout and listen for the echo. It's called echolocation, and much of it is far too high for you to hear.

scenes.label: Mouse: ~70 kHz
scenes.say: Remember your limit? About 20,000 hertz. A cat, 64,000. A mouse, around 70,000.

scenes.label: 212 kHz
scenes.say: The highest bat call ever recorded? About 212,000 hertz. That's more than ten times higher than you can hear.
Bats use calls like that to find moths in the dark. Fast, silent to us, and deadly to the moth.

scenes.label: Arms race
scenes.say: But here's the twist. Moths have been listening back. Scientists call it an evolutionary arms race.

scenes.label: Retuning ears
scenes.say: Some moths can even retune their ears the moment they hear a bat, before the bat changes its call. Like guessing your opponent's next move.
Bats go higher, so moths can't hear them coming. Moths evolve to hear higher. And one moth just won.

scenes.label: Greater wax moth
scenes.say: Number one. The greater wax moth. A small moth that lives as a pest in beehives.
In 2013, scientists at the University of Strathclyde in Scotland tested its hearing. And it broke the record for every animal.

scenes.label: Pet store bugs
scenes.say: Get this. They bought the larvae from a company that sells them as treats for bug-eating pets. Then waited for them to grow up.

scenes.label: 300,000 Hz
scenes.say: They played sounds up to 300,000 hertz. And the moth's eardrums still vibrated. Its nerves still fired.

scenes.label: Love song: 80 kHz
scenes.say: Its sweet spot is around 80,000 hertz. That's the pitch of the male's love song, clicks he makes with his wings.

scenes.label: 15x your limit
scenes.say: 300,000. That's about fifteen times higher than you can hear. And higher than any bat has ever been recorded calling.

scenes.label: Old record: 150 kHz
scenes.say: The old insect record was a gypsy moth at about 150,000. This moth doubled it.

scenes.label: Only 4 cells
scenes.say: And here's the crazy part. Its ear is super simple. Just an eardrum with four sensing cells.

scenes.label: Song or bat?
scenes.say: And the scientists think that's the trick. Its eardrum stops shaking super fast, so it can tell a quick love song from a slower bat attack.
One of the scientists put it simply. This moth can hear the calls of any bat.
And 300,000 was just the highest they tested. So its real limit could be even higher.

scenes.label: The twist
scenes.say: Okay, so here's the twist I promised. All these super ears have one big enemy. Us.

scenes.label: Science, Nov 2026
scenes.say: This month, two scientists at Queen's University Belfast published a giant review in the journal Science.

scenes.label: 177 species
scenes.say: They combined 214 experiments on 177 species. Traffic, ships, machines. Human noise.

scenes.label: 80% affected
scenes.say: The result? In 80 percent of those species, noise changed their body or their behavior. Stress hormones, development, behavior.

scenes.label: 37% fewer animals
scenes.say: For every 100 animals living in quiet places, there were only about 63 in noisy ones. That's 37 percent fewer.

scenes.label: The noise trap
scenes.say: And here's the cruel part. Noise makes prey hide. But some hiding spots make the noise even louder. So the prey runs out, right where predators wait.

scenes.label: 2.5x effort
scenes.say: And predators? In noise they worked 2.5 times harder, but caught about 25 percent less prey. Think about the owl hunting by sound.
Even elephants notice. In a 2021 study, they got more careful when they felt human-made vibrations in the ground.

scenes.label: Quiet zones
scenes.say: The good news? The scientists say quiet zones, places with less noise, could help protect them.
So, which super ear surprised you most? The shark, the elephant, the owl, the bat, or the tiny moth? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: A Moth Hears 15 Times Higher Than You Can
short.description: The greater wax moth can hear sounds approaching 300,000 hertz, higher than any bat call ever recorded, with an ear that has only four sensing cells. The full countdown of the animals with the best hearing on Earth is on the channel. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: Why can this tiny moth hear higher than any bat can scream? It hears 300,000 hertz.

scenes.label: You: ~20 kHz
scenes.say: You top out around 20,000 hertz. So this moth hears about fifteen times higher than you.

scenes.label: Bat: 212 kHz
scenes.say: Bats hunt moths with high calls, up to about 212,000 hertz. Higher calls are harder for moths to hear.

scenes.label: Arms race
scenes.say: So moths evolved to hear higher. The old insect record was a gypsy moth, at about 150,000.

scenes.label: Only 4 cells
scenes.say: Then scientists tested the greater wax moth. Its ear is just an eardrum with four sensing cells. And it doubled the record.
And it's a pest that lives in beehives. Which animal hears best on Earth? Comment below.
So the best ears on Earth belong to a tiny moth. Which leaves one question.
